anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction semantics force the engine to touch more data or hold locks longer than the business requirement really needs.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, index, or partition design is mis-aligned with access patterns, forcing otherwise reasonable SQL into inefficient scans, lookups, or maintenance overhead.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport, listener, or connection-handling resources between client and database are saturated or unreliable, throttling session establishment and data transfer.

When these three root causes are active at the same time, their symptoms overlap and amplify one another. Chatty or bloated SQL generated by the application produces large result sets and long-running transactions; the poor schema and index design prevents the optimizer from finding selective access paths, inflating execution time and result size even further; the oversized data streams then traverse a congested or connection-starved network layer, causing additional round-trip latency, retransmissions, and connection pool exhaustion. Observable phenomena therefore include: a surge of slow-query log entries that also exhibit client-read waits; execution plans dominated by full scans combined with long application think-times; spikes in network RTT, retransmits, or socket queue depth exactly when large, non-covering queries run; prolonged transactions holding locks while waiting for network I/O; exponential growth in active sessions due to retry storms following connection timeouts; and erratic application response times that do not improve when only server-side tuning is attempted in isolation.

Causally, chatty or over-broad SQL increases both the volume and duration of data access. Because the underlying schema lacks the right indexes or partitions, each statement consumes more CPU and I/O, elongating execution and enlarging result sets. These heavier payloads must then traverse an already constrained network, which slows completion of result delivery and keeps server back-ends and locks open far longer than planned. The extended hold time further increases concurrency pressure, triggering additional retries and connection churn that worsen network congestion—creating a feedback loop in which logical workload inefficiencies, physical design gaps, and transport bottlenecks mutually reinforce, driving systemic performance collapse under both OLTP and analytical mixed workloads.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
